final.title: Model deprecation is a hidden workflow cost
final.body:
If you are deciding whether to automate a repeat job in a small business, model deprecation is one thing worth checking before you build.

In plain terms, it means the AI model behind a workflow can change or disappear later. That does not make automation a bad idea. It does mean the real cost is not just the first build. You also need to think about what happens if the model has to be swapped out or the workflow has to be rebuilt.

That is the hidden part: the owner compares today’s manual work with a bounded automation project, but the comparison is incomplete if it ignores future maintenance. If the workflow is low-stakes and easy to fix, that risk may be fine. If it sits in a critical process, it deserves more attention.

A practical next step is simple: ask, "If the model behind this automation disappeared in 12 months, how much work would it take to replace it?" If the answer is hard to estimate, the workflow may be too fragile for a first pass.

Bareni’s diagnostic is meant to surface that kind of fit question, alongside the recurring workflow, so the business owner can decide with open eyes. Human approval still stays in charge of the investment.

final.title: What model deprecation hides in a small-business workflow
final.body:
If you are deciding whether to automate a recurring workflow, model deprecation is one hidden cost to check. In plain English, it means the AI model you build on can change, be replaced, or be withdrawn later. If that happens, the workflow may need a rebuild.

That is not a reason to avoid automation. It is a reason to separate two questions: does this workflow deserve automation at all, and how much disruption can I tolerate if the model layer changes?

For a small business, that is the real threshold. A stable enough workflow can be a good fit even if the underlying model is not permanent. But if the process is brittle, or if the owner cannot afford surprise maintenance, the safer move may be to keep it manual for now or choose a setup with a clearer fallback.

Bareni’s diagnostic is meant to surface that kind of choice honestly: identify the recurring workflow, check whether AI fits, then scope the next step before anyone commits to build. The timing is an intended scope, not a promise. Human approval stays in charge.

Practical next step: pick one workflow you might automate and ask, “If the model behind this disappeared next year, what would I have to redo?” If the answer is messy, you have found the part worth discussing first.
